sections.h2: How do you sell a house fast in Marana, AZ?
sections.html:
A Marana seller moves fastest by picking a sale route first, either an agent listing or a direct cash sale, and then clearing the HOA, tax and title items that tend to hold up closings. Marana is a growing town northwest of Tucson with a lot of newer subdivisions, so check early whether your house is in an HOA.

The Census Bureau estimated 65,523 residents on July 1, 2025, up 26.2 percent from the April 2020 base. Owners occupy 83.7 percent of homes, and the median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 was $413,800, per QuickFacts. A listing exposes the house to the widest group of buyers. A cash sale can close without a lender's appraisal, so the schedule is mostly in your hands and the buyer's title company.

Line up these items before you accept an offer:

  • HOA name, manager and a recent assessment statement
  • Payoff letters for each loan or lien
  • Utility, solar lease or battery lease contacts, if any
  • Records of permitted work such as pools, casitas and patio covers
  • The current Pima County or Pinal County tax bill

sections.h2: What should sellers know about Marana's size and history?
sections.html:
Marana lies mostly in Pima County, with a small piece in Pinal County, and stretches along Interstate 10 from the county line to the Tucson city limits. It covers about 121 square miles of land among the Tortolita, Santa Catalina and Tucson mountains and includes the Dove Mountain area. Phoenix is roughly 90 minutes northwest by Interstate 10, per Wikipedia.

Farming shaped the place. The area was first called Postvale, and cotton, wheat, barley, alfalfa and pecans grew here. The town incorporated about 10 square miles in March 1977, and 1,500 residents elected the first council that August. A targeted annexation policy began in 1979. In 1992 the council annexed a corridor along Interstate 10, Ina Road and Thornydale Road, and the Pima County Superior Court upheld that annexation in 1994.

The town's own profile page describes Marana as a logistics location on Interstate 10 and the Union Pacific Railroad, with a regional general aviation airport and a planned downtown. It names the Ritz-Carlton at Dove Mountain, Heritage Park and the Santa Cruz River Path as local landmarks. Those features are what buyers cite when they compare Marana with other parts of the Tucson area.

sections.h2: Does flood history matter when selling a Marana house?
sections.html:
It can. Marana suffered severe flash flooding during Tropical Storm Claudia in 1962, and in 1983 Tropical Storm Octave flooded Marana and four other Arizona towns almost entirely. The Octave system is considered the cause of the worst flood in Pima County history.

Flood risk today varies lot by lot. A buyer, lender or insurer will want to know whether the property sits in a mapped FEMA floodplain, so look up your parcel before you list and keep any flood insurance paperwork handy. If the house is in an unincorporated area rather than inside town limits, Arizona's A.R.S. 33-422 applies to sellers of five or fewer parcels other than subdivided land. It requires a written affidavit of disclosure at least seven days before transfer, covering legal and physical access, road maintenance, floodplain status, utilities, wells and septic systems, and it gives the buyer a five-day right to rescind.

About 87 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. The mean commute is nearly 28 minutes, so mention highway access in your listing description.

sections.h2: What does an HOA mean for a Marana sale?
sections.html:
If the house is in a planned community, the HOA sets part of your timeline. Under A.R.S. 33-1806, once you accept an offer in a community of 50 or more properties you notify the association, and the association has ten days to send the buyer its bylaws, declaration, recent board minutes, budget, financial reports, assessment amounts and any unpaid lien or open violation. Smaller communities have the seller deliver the information within the same ten days.

The association may charge the seller up to $400 for the resale package and lien statement, plus up to $100 for a rush within 72 hours and $50 for an update after 30 days. Fees are collected at the close of escrow and cannot be charged twice for one transaction. The buyer signs a statement at closing acknowledging the community's covenants and assessments. Ask the HOA manager for the package early, because an unpaid assessment shows up as a lien that comes out of your proceeds.

sections.h2: Which Marana rules and records affect a sale?
sections.html:
Ask the Town's Development Services Center for the permit history on your address, especially for pools, casitas, solar and garage work, and close any open permits before a buyer's inspector finds them. The Town's short-term rental page sets the rules for short-term rentals. Requirements listed there include:

  • A Town business license for the rental
  • A valid Transaction Privilege Tax number from the state
  • Registration with the Pima County Assessor
  • A neighbor notification attestation emailed to licensing@maranaaz.gov before the rental start date
  • Annual renewal, with an invoice mailed 30 days before expiration, and updates to the Town within 10 days of any change

If you have operated a short-term rental, give the buyer the license and registration details. A buyer who plans to rent should ask the Town's licensing staff what a new application needs.

sections.h2: How are deeds recorded and property taxes billed for Marana homes?
sections.html:
Most Marana deeds are recorded with the Pima County Recorder. The fee page lists a flat $30 recording fee under A.R.S. 11-475 and a $5 fee to return documents submitted improperly. It says the Affidavit of Property Value form comes from the Arizona Department of Revenue. State law requires the affidavit with a transfer deed unless the deed shows an exemption, under A.R.S. 11-1133. For the small part of Marana in Pinal County, the Pinal County Recorder charges $30 for any document, and that fee already covers the affidavit of property value.

Pima County sent its 2026 bills by the end of September. Its property tax page lists these dates:

  • First half due October 1, 2026, delinquent November 2, 2026. That date has passed.
  • Full-year payment due December 31, 2026.
  • Second half due March 1, 2027, delinquent May 3, 2027.

The Pima Treasurer's office takes online payments at to.pima.gov or by phone at 520-724-8341, and charges a 1.95 percent convenience fee on card payments with a $1.95 minimum, or $0.50 for an eCheck. Address changes for tax bills go through the Pima County Assessor. Pinal County parcels follow Pinal's own schedule, with the first half delinquent after 5 p.m. on November 1 and the second half after May 1.

Most of the town is in the Marana Unified School District, which serves grades preK to 12 from an office at 11279 W. Grier Road. Flowing Wells Unified covers the far southeastern edge of the town, and the portion in Pinal County is served by Red Rock Elementary and Santa Cruz Valley Union High School districts. Confirm the district with a street address search before you list.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Marana house with an HOA lien or unpaid assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. The HOA's resale statement lists any unpaid assessment lien, and your escrow officer can pay it from your proceeds if you agree. Ask the association for its statement early, since the association has ten days after notice of a pending sale to deliver the resale package to the buyer.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed for a Marana property?
faqs.a: The Pima County Recorder lists $30 per document, and the Pinal County Recorder lists the same $30. The Affidavit of Property Value is required unless the deed shows an exemption. Your escrow or title company normally pays and files these at closing.

faqs.q: Is Marana in Pima County or Pinal County?
faqs.a: Mostly Pima County, with a small portion in Pinal County. Pima County bills most Marana homes, while the Pinal County Treasurer bills parcels in the Pinal portion. Look at your tax statement to see which county issues your bill and which due dates apply.

faqs.q: Did I miss the first-half property tax deadline for Marana in 2026?
faqs.a: If your home is in Pima County, the first half was due October 1 and became delinquent after November 2, 2026, which has passed. Interest accrues after that date. Check the Pima Treasurer's site for the exact amount. If you have not paid, paying both halves by December 31 waives interest accrued after November 1.

Yes, with a Town business license. The owner needs a Transaction Privilege Tax number, Pima County Assessor registration and a neighbor notification attestation before the rental starts. Licenses renew each year, and changes must be reported to the Town within 10 days.
